fields.title: Men Who Tended the Flock
fields.description: Discover the raw, biblical heart of the pastoral calling: feeding the hungry, seeking the lost, and guarding the flock. Whether you are a seasoned leader or a curious seeker, these stories will ignite a deeper love for the Good Shepherd and His people.

qa.question: What is Men Who Tended the Flock about?
qa.answer: It opens up the biblical heart of the pastoral calling — feeding the hungry, seeking the lost, and guarding the flock — through the lives of faithful shepherds of God's people. Whether for a seasoned leader or a curious seeker, the book's stories are meant to kindle a deeper love for the Good Shepherd and for the people he entrusts to his under-shepherds.

qa.question: What is the 'pastoral calling' the book describes?
qa.answer: The work of a shepherd over God's people: feeding them with truth, seeking out the straying and the lost, guarding the flock against danger, and caring for the weak and hurting. The book draws this pattern from Scripture's own shepherd imagery, holding up the tending of souls as a high and costly calling modelled on Christ himself.

qa.question: How does the book teach the pastoral life?
qa.answer: Chiefly through stories — the lives of men who tended God's flock faithfully — rather than through abstract instruction. By showing the pastoral calling lived out, the book both teaches what it involves and stirs affection for it, letting real examples of shepherding ignite in the reader a deeper love for the work and for the people it serves.

qa.question: Who is the Good Shepherd the book points to?
qa.answer: Jesus Christ, who called himself the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. The book presents every faithful human shepherd as an under-shepherd of Christ, drawing their pattern and power from him, so that the aim of the stories is not merely to admire pastors but to deepen the reader's love for the Shepherd they serve.

qa.question: Who is the book written for?
qa.answer: Both 'seasoned leaders' and 'curious seekers' — pastors and Christian leaders who bear the shepherd's burden, and ordinary believers who want to understand and value the pastoral calling. Its stories speak to anyone who cares about how God's people are fed, sought, and guarded, and about the heart the work requires.

qa.question: What does the book say the pastoral heart looks like?
qa.answer: A heart that feeds the hungry, seeks the lost, and guards the flock — patient, self-giving, and shaped by love for the sheep and for their Shepherd. The book presents the calling as 'raw' and biblical rather than professional or polished, rooted in the costly care that Scripture describes and that Christ embodied.

qa.question: How does it fit with the companion 'men' collections?
qa.answer: It is one of a family of collections holding up different facets of faithful Christian manhood and calling — men of prayer, men who moved heaven, men who gave everything, and here men who tended the flock. Together they gather examples that stir the reader toward wholehearted devotion, this one focusing on the shepherd's particular work of caring for God's people.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning, or with whichever life draws them, since the chapters largely stand on their own. Read together, the stories build a portrait of the pastoral calling meant to kindle love for the Good Shepherd and his flock, so the book rewards being read reflectively rather than merely for information.

fields.title: Introduction: The Weight and the Glory of the Pastoral Calling
fields.body_html:
There is no calling quite like it. The pastor stands at the intersection of the eternal and the ordinary — one foot in the theological library, the other in the hospital room; one hand on the Scripture, the other on the shoulder of someone whose world has just fallen apart. He is simultaneously a student, a preacher, a counsellor, a comforter, a leader, and a servant. He carries the weight of souls. He is responsible, under God, for the spiritual nourishment and protection of people who will one day stand before the Almighty — and he knows it. The men in this book felt that weight, accepted it, and by the grace of God discharged it with a faithfulness that history has not been able to forget.

The pastoral calling is not a human invention. It flows directly from the heart of God, who revealed Himself, across the whole span of Scripture, as a shepherd. The imagery is everywhere.

Isaiah heard the divine promise: “He tends his flock like a shepherd: He gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them close to his heart; he gently leads those that have young” (Isaiah 40:11, NIV). Before He gave the church its human under-shepherds, God established His own shepherding character as the pattern they would be called to imitate. Every pastor who has ever wept with a grieving widow, searched for a wandering soul, or patiently fed the spiritually starving was doing so as a reflection of the God who is Himself the first and greatest Shepherd.

God was not reluctant to hold human shepherds accountable for the care of His flock. Ezekiel recorded some of the most piercing words in the prophetic literature — words addressed not to pagans but to Israel’s own leaders: “Woe to you shepherds of Israel who only take care of yourselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock? You eat the curds, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the choice animals, but you do not take care of the flock. You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. You have not brought back the strays or searched for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:2–4, NIV). This divine indictment is also, read from the opposite direction, the most comprehensive job description for faithful pastoral ministry ever written. The good shepherd does precisely everything here described as neglected.

What is a good pastor? He is not primarily a motivational speaker, a nonprofit executive, or a spiritual entertainer. He is a man called by God to feed, protect, lead, and love a specific group of people entrusted to his care — not for a season of personal ambition but for the long haul of faithful ministry. The ten men in this book were not uniformly gifted, equally educated, or similarly temperamented. Chrysostom thundered from the great pulpit of Constantinople and was exiled for refusing to flatter the powerful. George Herbert composed poetry in a country village and died at thirty-nine having transformed it. Richard Baxter visited every home in Kidderminster with a catechism and a burning conviction that no soul in his parish should perish for want of a shepherd’s attention. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal underground seminary and went to the gallows rather than compromise the integrity of the church he had served.

The apostle Paul’s charge to the Ephesian elders remains the definitive description of what the pastoral calling demands: “Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood” (Acts 20:28, NIV). Two things are inseparable in this command: the pastor must first keep watch over himself — his own soul, his own walk with God, his own integrity — and then over the flock. A man cannot give what he does not possess. A shepherd whose own soul is malnourished will soon be unable to feed those in his care. The men in this book understood this.

Their pastoral fruitfulness was inseparable from their personal devotion.

Peter’s instruction to elders carries both the weight of command and the warmth of invitation: “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them — not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away” (1 Peter 5:2–4, NIV). That final promise — the unfading crown from the Chief Shepherd’s own hand — is what sustained these ten men through decades of invisible, costly, often thankless ministry. They were not working for human applause. They were working for an audience of One.

These chapters are not hagiographies. They do not pretend these men were without flaw or failure. Several of them made serious mistakes; some were imperfect in ways their own writings acknowledge with painful candor. What they shared was not perfection but a profound seriousness about the pastoral calling — a conviction that to be entrusted with the care of souls was the most solemn responsibility a human being could bear, and a determination to discharge it, by the grace of God, with everything they had.

These pages are written for pastors and for those who love them. They are written for seminarians who are still deciding what kind of minister they will be, for elders who wonder whether the quiet faithfulness of their ministry matters, and for church members who want to understand the calling of the man who stands before them week by week. Above all, they are written for anyone who aspires to shepherd — in whatever form, at whatever scale — in the spirit of the One who said, “I am the good shepherd.”

fields.title: John Chrysostom — The Golden-Mouthed Shepherd
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

John Chrysostom was born around 347 AD in Antioch, Syria, the son of a military officer, and received the finest classical education his era could provide before his conversion to an ascetic Christian life under the bishop Meletius. He spent several formative years as a monk in the Syrian desert before returning to Antioch, where his gifts as a preacher drew enormous crowds and earned him the posthumous title by which history remembers him: Chrysostom, “Golden-Mouthed.” In 398 AD, the Emperor Arcadius appointed him Archbishop of Constantinople against his will, and Chrysostom accepted the role with the same directness he brought to everything: he immediately sold the extravagant furnishings of the episcopal palace and used the proceeds to build hospitals for the poor, dismissed corrupt clergy, and began preaching — to the empress and the beggar with identical plain-spokenness — every Sunday. His refusal to flatter the powerful resulted in two exiles, the second of which killed him; he died in 407 AD on a forced march in the mountains of Pontus.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Chrysostom’s masterpiece on pastoral ministry, “On the Priesthood,” written early in his career, remains one of the most penetrating analyses of the pastoral calling in Christian literature. Its central argument is deceptively simple: the care of souls is the most demanding, the most consequential, and the most dangerous of all human occupations. It demands more than medicine, more than law, more than statecraft, because its territory is the eternal soul, and its failures are measured not in earthly loss but in loss that cannot be undone. Chrysostom did not write this to discourage pastors but to call them to a level of seriousness commensurate with the stakes.

The foundation of Chrysostom’s pastoral vision was the understanding that the congregation was not the pastor’s audience but his flock — a living body for which he was, under Christ, responsible. He drew the sharpest possible contrast between the pastor and the hireling from Jesus’ own words: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

The hired hand is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep. So when he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away.” (John 10:11–12, NIV). The test of the true shepherd, Chrysostom taught, came not when the ministry was easy and the congregation was growing, but when the wolves arrived — when standing firm cost something real. He himself passed this test at the cost of his life.

Chrysostom was equally insistent that faithful preaching was the non-negotiable center of pastoral ministry. A shepherd who did not feed the flock with the Word was a shepherd in name only. He preached verse by verse through entire books of the Bible in an era when that practice was unusual, convinced that the congregation needed the whole counsel of God, not a curated selection. He took Paul’s charge with absolute literalism: “Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; correct, rebuke and encourage — with great patience and careful instruction” (2 Timothy 4:2, NIV). His own sermons, preserved in eighty-nine homilies on Matthew and sixty-eight on Genesis among hundreds of others, were the living embodiment of this command. They were not rhetorical performances but pastoral acts — careful, sustained, patient feeding of a flock.

His pastoral theology of the poor was among his most distinctive and demanding contributions.

Chrysostom believed that the way a congregation treated the poor was a direct measure of how seriously it had understood the gospel. His homily on Matthew 25 — in which he drew out the staggering implication that Christ was present in the person of every hungry, thirsty, and homeless person — was among the most socially urgent pastoral sermons in Christian history.

He wrote: “Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked. Do not pay him homage in the temple clad in silk only then to neglect him outside where he suffers cold and nakedness.” He grounded this not in social theory but in Paul’s declaration: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, NIV). The pastoral community that took this verse seriously, he argued, could not be indifferent to the material suffering of any of its members.

Chrysostom was also the great pastoral theologian of courage. He watched too many pastors around him perform a careful calculus of how much truth they could afford to preach without offending those whose patronage sustained the church. He found this kind of ministry beneath contempt. The pastor’s obligation was not to his social standing but to the souls in his care, and those souls needed the truth even — especially — when the truth was unwelcome.

He held to Paul’s warning with unflinching consistency: “For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear” (2 Timothy 4:3, NIV). Chrysostom refused to be one of those teachers. His two exiles were the price he paid for that refusal, and he paid it without complaint.

His final pastoral legacy was the example of his own death. Driven by soldiers through the mountains in the bitter autumn cold, too weak to walk, he died with the same words on his lips that had opened his ministry: “Glory be to God for all things.” It was a pastoral death in the fullest sense — a dying that preached. He had taught his congregation throughout his ministry that suffering was not a contradiction of God’s love but a participation in Christ’s. Now he showed them what that looked like in a man who believed it. He had lived Paul’s testimony: “I have learned to be content whatever the circumstances” (Philippians 4:11, NIV). He had. And he had taught his flock, by word and by example, to do the same.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, the Good Shepherd, give us the courage of Chrysostom — to preach the Word when it is welcome and when it is not, to stand between our people and the wolves regardless of the cost, and to love the poor not as a project but as Yourself. Make us shepherds who are willing to lay down our comfort, our reputation, and our ease in the service of the flock You have entrusted to our care.

Amen.

fields.title: Gregory the Great — The Servant of Servants
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Gregory was born around 540 AD in Rome into one of the city’s most distinguished aristocratic families, and by his early thirties had risen to become the Prefect of Rome — the highest civil office in the city. At the height of his civic career, he underwent a dramatic conversion to the monastic life, transforming his family’s estate on the Caelian Hill into a monastery and spending five years in the contemplative life he had always preferred. Against his own wishes, Pope Pelagius II drew him out of the monastery for diplomatic service and then, in 590 AD, the clergy and people of Rome elected Gregory himself as pope. He accepted with genuine grief — describing himself in his letters as having been dragged from the contemplative life into “the sea of the world” — but went on to govern the Western church for the next fourteen years with a competence and pastoral wisdom that made him, in the judgment of history, not merely “Great” but the defining model of Christian pastoral leadership for the next thousand years. He styled himself “Servant of the servants of God,” a title still used by the papacy today.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Gregory’s pastoral treatise, the “Liber Regulae Pastoralis” (Book of Pastoral Rule), written in the first months of his papacy, is perhaps the single most influential handbook on pastoral ministry in Christian history. King Alfred the Great translated it into Old English. It shaped the understanding of ministry across the medieval church. Its central insight — that the pastor must know each sheep differently and therefore minister differently to each one — remains as challenging and true today as when Gregory wrote it. Good pastoral care, he argued, is not the application of a single method to all people, but the discernment of what each person, in their particular condition, most needs from God.

Gregory’s foundational pastoral conviction was rooted in the shepherd imagery of the Hebrew prophets, particularly the great shepherd-chapter of Ezekiel. The divine promise in Ezekiel 34 was, for Gregory, not merely a prophetic description of Christ but a blueprint for what human under-shepherds were to imitate: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will shepherd the flock with justice” (Ezekiel 34:16, NIV). Each verb in this verse was for Gregory a pastoral obligation: to search, to bring back, to bind up, to strengthen, to exercise justice. The good pastor was active, not passive — going out to the lost rather than waiting for them to return, binding wounds rather than ignoring them, strengthening the weak rather than merely celebrating the strong.

The most practically transformative dimension of Gregory’s pastoral teaching was his insistence on differentiated care. The frightened person needed encouragement; the arrogant person needed correction. The poor person needed comfort; the rich person needed warning. The healthy person needed instruction; the sick person needed patience. Applying the same pastoral approach to all of these was not pastoral wisdom but pastoral laziness. He found the model for this differentiation in Paul’s description of his own ministry: “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, NIV). This was not inconsistency or sycophancy — it was pastoral intelligence, the skill of knowing what medicine was needed for what condition.

Gregory’s theology of pastoral humility was equally profound. He held the highest office in the Western church and chose for his title words that deliberately inverted the logic of human power: “Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be your slave — just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:26–28, NIV). Gregory believed that pastoral authority was not diminished by humble service but constituted by it. The bishop who used his office to accumulate privilege was not exercising pastoral authority; he was evacuating it. The servant of the servants was, precisely in his servanthood, the most truly authoritative figure in the room.

Gregory also understood the pastoral office as demanding the highest standard of personal spiritual life. The pastor could not call his flock to a depth of devotion he himself had not entered. This was not merely a matter of credibility but of capacity: a man who had not spent time in contemplative prayer could not lead others into it, and a man who had not wrestled with his own sin could not speak with genuine authority to the sin of others. Gregory grounded this in Paul’s instruction to Timothy, which he regarded as the most important pastoral exhortation in the New Testament: “Watch your life and doctrine closely. Persevere in them, because if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16, NIV). Life and doctrine together: the pastoral office demanded excellence in both, and neither could substitute for the other.

His personal pastoral style — accessible, attentive, patient, and formidably competent — was itself a teaching. He wrote over eight hundred letters that survive, many of them pastoral responses to specific individuals in specific crises. He responded to the plague, organized food distribution, negotiated with the Lombards, reformed the liturgy, and sent missionaries to England — all while sustaining a personal spiritual life that he described as always being interrupted and never being abandoned. He embodied Peter’s vision of pastoral leadership: “Not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3, NIV). He was the example — in service, in humility, in competence, and in the willingness to be spent for the sake of those in his care.

A Prayer

Lord, You are the Shepherd who searches, binds up, and strengthens. Make us pastors in Your image — not servants of our own comfort or reputation, but servants of Your servants. Give us Gregory’s discernment to know what each soul needs, his humility to stoop to every need, and his perseverance to sustain the caring over the long years of ministry. Let us be examples to the flock by becoming nothing less than what we preach. Amen.

He styled himself “Servant of the servants of God,” a title still used by the papacy today. His Vision for the Pastoral Calling Gregory’s pastoral treatise, the “Liber Regulae Pastoralis” (Book of Pastoral Rule), written in the first months of his papacy, is perhaps the single most influential handbook on pastoral ministry in Christian history. King Alfred the Great translated it into Old English. It shaped the understanding of ministry across the medieval church. Its central insight — that the pastor must know each sheep differently and therefore minister differently to each one — remains as challenging and true today as when Gregory wrote it. Good pastoral care, he argued, is not the application of a single method to all people, but the discernment of what each person, in their particular condition, most needs from God. Gregory’s foundational pastoral conviction was rooted in the shepherd imagery of the Hebrew prophets, particularly the great shepherd-chapter of Ezekiel. The divine promise in Ezekiel 34 was, for Gregory, not merely a prophetic description of Christ but a blueprint for what human under-shepherds were to imitate: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will shepherd the flock with justice” (Ezekiel 34:16, NIV). Each verb in this verse was for Gregory a pastoral obligation: to search, to bring back, to bind up, to strengthen, to exercise justice. The good pastor was active, not passive — going out to the lost rather than waiting for them to return, binding wounds rather than ignoring them, strengthening the weak rather than merely celebrating the strong. The most practically transformative dimension of Gregory’s pastoral teaching was his insistence on differentiated care. The frightened person needed encouragement; the arrogant person needed correction. The poor person needed comfort; the rich person needed warning. The healthy person needed instruction; the sick person needed patience. Applying the same pastoral approach to all of these was not pastoral wisdom but pastoral laziness. He found the model for this differentiation in Paul’s description of his own ministry: “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, NIV). This was not inconsistency or sycophancy — it was pastoral intelligence, the skill of knowing what medicine was needed for what condition. Gregory’s theology of pastoral humility was equally profound. He held the highest office in the Western church and chose for his title words that deliberately inverted the logic of human power: “Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be your slave — just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:26–28, NIV). Gregory believed that pastoral authority was not diminished by humble service but constituted by it. The bishop who used his office to accumulate privilege was not exercising pastoral authority; he was evacuating it. The servant of the servants was, precisely in his servanthood, the most truly authoritative figure in the room. Gregory also understood the pastoral office as demanding the highest standard of personal spiritual life. The pastor could not call his flock to a depth of devotion he himself had not entered. This was not merely a matter of credibility but of capacity: a man who had not spent time in contemplative prayer could not lead others into it, and a man who had not wrestled with his own sin could not speak with genuine authority to the sin of others. Gregory grounded this in Paul’s instruction to Timothy, which he regarded as the most important pastoral exhortation in the New Testament: “Watch your life and doctrine closely. Persevere in them, because if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16, NIV). Life and doctrine together: the pastoral office demanded excellence in both, and neither could substitute for the other. His personal pastoral style — accessible, attentive, patient, and formidably competent — was itself a teaching. He wrote over eight hundred letters that survive, many of them pastoral responses to specific individuals in specific crises. He responded to the plague, organized food distribution, negotiated with the Lombards, reformed the liturgy, and sent missionaries to England — all while sustaining a personal spiritual life that he described as always being interrupted and never being abandoned. He embodied Peter’s vision of pastoral leadership: “Not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3, NIV). He was the example — in service, in humility, in competence, and in the willingness to be spent for the sake of those in his care. A Prayer Lord, You are the Shepherd who searches, binds up, and strengthens. Make us pastors in Your image — not servants of our own comfort or reputation, but servants of Your servants. Give us Gregory’s discernment to know what each soul needs, his humility to stoop to every need, and his perseverance to sustain the caring over the long years of ministry. Let us be examples to the flock by becoming nothing less than what we preach. Amen.

fields.title: George Herbert — The Country Parson Who Made the Ordinary Holy
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

George Herbert was born on April 3, 1593, in Montgomery, Wales, into a distinguished English family and received a brilliant education at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was eventually appointed Public Orator — a position that brought him into regular contact with the court of King James I and seemed to promise a career of worldly prominence.

He resisted the call to pastoral ministry for years, reluctant to leave the prestige of public life, but in 1630, at the age of thirty-six, he accepted the small country rectorship of Bemerton in Wiltshire, near Salisbury. He had at most three years left to live — he died of tuberculosis in 1633 at thirty-nine — but those three years produced what many regard as the most beautiful body of devotional poetry in the English language and a prose guide to country pastoral ministry, “A Priest to the Temple, or The Country Parson,” which remains a model of pastoral humility, attentiveness, and creativity to this day.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Herbert’s understanding of pastoral ministry was inseparable from his sacramental imagination: the conviction that the ordinary materials of human life — a meal, a field, a broom, a bed — were capable of carrying the weight of divine meaning. This was not mysticism but incarnational theology: the God who had taken on flesh and dwelt in a village was the God who was present in the daily textures of his parishioners’ lives, and the pastor’s task was to help them see Him there.

The country parson was not a figure who descended periodically from spiritual heights to address the mundane; he was one who lived among his people and helped them discover the sacred in their midst.

Herbert’s portrait of the country parson in his prose work is striking in its emphasis on pastoral presence. The pastor must be known to his people not as an occasional visitor or a Sunday institution but as a neighbour, a friend, and a fellow laborer in the same soil. He drew on Paul’s tender image of the nursing mother: “Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8, NIV). This sharing of life — not merely of information — was, Herbert believed, what distinguished pastoral ministry from lecturing. The pastor who shared his life with his people loved them in the way Paul described: not as an audience to be instructed but as children to be nurtured.

He insisted in The Country Parson that the pastoral home should itself be a sermon. The parson’s household was to be governed by prayer, hospitality, simplicity, and godly order, so that anyone who entered it felt the presence of a different set of values from those that governed the world outside. The parson’s wife was his partner in this ministry; his children were its first fruits; his table was open to the poorest parishioner. Herbert grounded this conviction in Paul’s requirements for the overseer: “An overseer is to be above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness” (1 Timothy 3:2–3, NIV). These were not abstract virtues for Herbert but practical habits of daily life — each one, practiced consistently, shaping the home into a visible argument for the gospel.

Herbert’s pastoral poetry — collected in The Temple, published posthumously — was itself a pastoral instrument. He wrote poems that gave his parishioners language for experiences they had felt but could not articulate: the experience of spiritual dryness, of feeling unworthy of God’s love, of struggling to pray, of discovering that God had been present in circumstances they had assumed He had abandoned. His great poem “Love (III)” — in which Love (Christ) welcomes the reluctant soul to the table despite its protests of unworthiness — captured in fourteen lines what Paul took a chapter to unfold: “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16, NIV).

Herbert’s pastoral genius was in translating these enormous truths into the textures of human experience that his parishioners actually lived.

He was also a pastor of great personal patience with the struggling, the slow, and the spiritually confused. He wrote in The Country Parson that the parson must never show frustration with those who do not understand quickly, must never make them feel stupid for their questions, and must always remember that he himself was once ignorant of the things he now knows. He found his model for this in Paul’s instruction: “And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful. Opponents must be gently instructed, in the hope that God will grant them repentance leading them to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:24–25, NIV). Gentleness in instruction was not a pastoral nicety for Herbert but a theological conviction: the God who had been patient with him required him to be patient with others.

Herbert died at thirty-nine with a short ministry behind him and a handful of poems sent to a friend with the instruction that they be published only if he thought they might help “some poor dejected soul.” They have been helping poor dejected souls for nearly four hundred years. He had discharged the pastoral calling in the way Paul described: “We proclaim him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28, NIV). He had proclaimed, admonished, and taught — in sermons, in prose, in verse, and in the daily texture of a life lived among his people. The maturity he labored for in others was achieved in himself by the grace of the God he served.

A Prayer

Lord of the ordinary and the holy, teach us to find You in the textures of everyday life and to help others find You there too. Where we are tempted to consider small ministries beneath us, give us Herbert’s contentment with the particular flock You have given us. Make our homes sermons, our tables open, our patience inexhaustible, and our words — however few — capable of helping some poor dejected soul find their way to You. Amen.

fields.title: Richard Baxter — The Reformed Pastor Who Visited Every Door
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Richard Baxter was born on November 12, 1615, in Rowton, Shropshire, England, the son of a gentleman farmer whose own late conversion to genuine Christian faith shaped young Richard’s understanding of what real religion looked like. Largely self-educated in theology through voracious reading, he was ordained and in 1641 became the minister of Kidderminster — a town of two thousand people that by his own account was, when he arrived, almost entirely irreligious.

By the time he left fourteen years later, the town had been transformed: almost every house had a family altar, the streets rang with the sounds of singing, and the congregation had grown to such numbers that the church could not contain them. He accomplished this not by dramatic revival meetings but by systematic, patient, personal pastoral visitation of every family in the town. His book “The Reformed Pastor,” published in 1656, remains the most searching examination of pastoral duty in the English language.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Baxter’s pastoral vision was built on a single, burning conviction: every soul in the parish was his responsibility before God. Not the souls who attended faithfully. Not the souls who were easy to reach. Every soul. This was not a pious aspiration for Baxter but a methodological commitment he discharged by meeting with every family in Kidderminster — roughly eight hundred families — once per year, catechizing them personally, assessing their spiritual state, and addressing whatever he found with teaching, exhortation, and prayer. He described this work as the heart of his ministry, more important than any sermon he preached.

The theological foundation of Baxter’s pastoral urgency was the doctrine of the watchman from Ezekiel — one of the most searching passages in the whole of Scripture for those who hold pastoral responsibility: “When I say to a wicked person, ‘You will surely die,’ and you do not warn them or speak out to dissuade them from their evil ways in order to save their life, that wicked person will die for their sin, and I will hold you accountable for their blood. But if you do warn the wicked person and they do not turn from their wickedness or from their evil ways, they will die for their sin; but you will have saved yourself” (Ezekiel 3:18–19, NIV). Baxter took this with deadly seriousness. The blood of souls who perished for want of a shepherd’s warning would be required of the shepherd. This was not a comfortable doctrine, but Baxter did not seek comfort in his theology — he sought fidelity.

His most famous line from The Reformed Pastor crystallizes his entire pastoral philosophy: “I preached as never sure to preach again, and as a dying man to dying men.” This was not hyperbole. Baxter was ill for most of his ministry, frequently certain that he was close to death, and he preached accordingly. Every sermon was potentially his last. Every visit to a family might be the last opportunity to speak to that soul before it stood before God. This urgency was not manufactured anxiety but a theological conviction that time was short and eternity was long, and that the pastor who forgot this fact was unworthy of his calling. He took Paul’s charge with complete literalism: “In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom, I give you this charge: Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:1–2, NIV). It was always the season.

Baxter was equally insistent about the pastor’s own spiritual state as a prerequisite for effective pastoral ministry. He opened The Reformed Pastor with a searching section on the necessity of personal godliness in the minister, arguing that a pastor who neglected his own soul was not merely personally compromised but pastorally disabled. He quoted Acts 20:28 and then unpacked its first clause with piercing intensity: “Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers” (Acts 20:28, NIV). “Yourselves” came first. A man who could not keep watch over his own soul had no business claiming to watch over others.

This was not an optional preliminary to pastoral ministry; it was its precondition.

His model of catechetical visitation — meeting with families in their homes, working through questions about faith and salvation, identifying misunderstandings and addressing them with Scripture — was driven by a theology of every-member accountability that he found in the New Testament pattern of mutual instruction. He loved Paul’s confidence in the Roman congregation: “I myself am convinced, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with knowledge and competent to instruct one another” (Romans 15:14, NIV).

The goal of his personal pastoral work was precisely this — to bring his parishioners to the point of being able to instruct and exhort one another. He was working toward his own relative redundancy. When every home in Kidderminster could sustain its own spiritual life, he had done his job.

Baxter’s pastoral legacy was the proof that genuine, systematic pastoral work transforms communities. He did not wait for revival to come to Kidderminster; he believed that faithful pastoral labor was the ordinary means by which God brought revival, and he labored accordingly. His confidence rested on God’s own promise through Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will lead you with knowledge and understanding” (Jeremiah 3:15, NIV). The shepherd God gives after His own heart leads with knowledge and understanding — not raw enthusiasm, not institutional management, but the patient, informed, personally attentive leadership of a man who knows his sheep by name. Baxter knew every family in Kidderminster. He knew their names, their struggles, their questions, and their spiritual condition. And through that knowledge, God transformed the town.

A Prayer

Lord, make us shepherds who feel the weight of every soul in our care. Deliver us from the comfortable deception that faithful preaching alone discharges the pastoral calling, and drive us out of our offices and into our people’s homes. Give us Baxter’s urgency — to preach as dying men to dying men — and his patience, to visit, to catechize, to pray, and to work as though the next visit might be the one that opens a door that has been closed for years. Amen.

fields.title: Jonathan Edwards — The Theologian Who Tended His Flock
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Jonathan Edwards was born on October 5, 1703, in East Windsor, Connecticut, the son of a Congregational minister and the grandson of the formidable Solomon Stoddard of Northampton.

He entered Yale at thirteen, graduated at seventeen, and by 1727 had joined his grandfather’s congregation in Northampton, Massachusetts, as associate pastor. He succeeded Stoddard in 1729 and remained in Northampton for over twenty years until his congregation dismissed him in 1750 in a bitter dispute over communion practice — a rejection he bore with remarkable grace. He spent the following years as a frontier missionary to Native Americans at Stockbridge before being elected president of the College of New Jersey (now Princeton) in 1757. He died in 1758, six weeks after his installation, of a smallpox inoculation gone wrong, at the age of fifty-four. He is widely regarded as the greatest theologian and philosopher that America has produced, but he was, first and throughout, a pastor.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Edwards’ pastoral vision was inseparable from his theological vision, because he believed that the deepest pastoral act was the communication of truth about God in all its depth and beauty and terror. A congregation that understood who God was — truly, deeply, not merely notionally — would love Him appropriately, fear Him appropriately, and live accordingly. The pastor’s primary task was therefore theological: to bring his people into genuine, transforming knowledge of the God they professed to worship. Sermons that did not engage the mind and the heart together, he believed, produced only a superficial religion that would not survive the pressures of the world.

Edwards’ understanding of his pastoral role was shaped by Paul’s magnificent description of the minister’s comprehensive aim: “He is the one we proclaim, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ. To this end I strenuously contend with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in me” (Colossians 1:28–29, NIV). “Fully mature in Christ” was not a modest target. It required nothing less than the comprehensive transformation of the whole person — mind, will, affections, and habits — in conformity with the image of Christ. Edwards worked toward this goal in Northampton for over two decades, preaching, teaching, counseling, and writing, always aiming at maturity rather than mere attendance.

The revival of 1734–1735 in Northampton, which Edwards documented in A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God, presented him with the pastoral challenge he was perhaps best equipped to meet: how to distinguish genuine spiritual awakening from emotional counterfeit.

His response was the most careful and theologically sophisticated pastoral discernment of religious experience that the Protestant tradition had yet produced. He found his categories in Scripture: “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–22, NIV). He refused to quench the Spirit by dismissing everything unusual as mere enthusiasm; he also refused to accept everything emotional as therefore genuine. His Treatise Concerning Religious Affections remains the definitive pastoral guide to this kind of discernment.

Edwards also understood the pastoral office as demanding the most complete and unflinching proclamation of the whole counsel of God — including the doctrines that made polite society uncomfortable. His famous sermon “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” is often caricatured as theological sadism, but it was in fact a pastoral act of desperate love: the attempt to break through the complacency of a congregation that was dangerously comfortable with a religion that cost them nothing. He was doing precisely what Paul charged: “For I have not hesitated to proclaim to you the whole will of God” (Acts 20:27, NIV). The whole will of God included judgment, and a pastor who omitted it was not protecting his congregation from unnecessary discomfort but exposing them to eternal danger.

His pastoral care in the aftermath of his 1750 dismissal is one of the most revealing episodes of his ministry. He had been rejected by the congregation he had served for twenty-three years. The dismissal was painful, public, and, by most historical assessments, unjust. Yet he left Northampton without bitterness, commended his congregation to God’s mercy, and continued to pray for them. fields.title: John Newton — The Former Slave Trader Who Shepherded with Grace
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

John Newton was born on August 4, 1725, in London, the son of a ship captain, and spent his early adult years in the brutal world of the Atlantic slave trade — first as a pressed sailor, then as a crewman, and finally as the captain of slave ships. A terrifying storm in 1748 precipitated the crisis that began his conversion, and he was ordained as a Church of England minister in 1764, serving as curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire until 1780. He co-authored with William Cowper the famous “Olney Hymns,” including “Amazing Grace,” and corresponded with hundreds of individuals across England — producing some of the warmest and most practically wise pastoral letters in the English language. He spent the last twenty-seven years of his ministry as rector of St. Mary Woolnoth in London, where he continued to preach and counsel until near his death in 1807 at the age of eighty-two.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Newton’s pastoral identity was inseparable from his personal history. He was, by his own lifelong testimony, the greatest evidence for the proposition that God’s grace was greater than any sin — a fact he could not allow himself to forget and would not allow his congregation to forget. His famous self-description in his will — “John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy” — was not false modesty but the controlling narrative of his entire pastoral ministry. He had been the chief of sinners. He therefore had the deepest possible sympathy for the struggling.

The pastoral letters Newton wrote across his long ministry constitute one of the richest bodies of practical spiritual direction in the English language. They were remarkable for their combination of doctrinal precision and pastoral warmth — never separating the two, never allowing doctrine to become cold or warmth to become sentimental. He operated from the apostolic pattern Paul described: “We were gentle among you, like a mother caring for her little children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7, NIV). This gentleness was not the gentleness of someone who had never known real darkness, but of someone who had known it deeply and had been reached anyway.

He could write to those in spiritual despair with genuine authority: he had been there.

One of Newton’s most distinctive pastoral contributions was his theology of the slow work of grace in the Christian life. He was unimpressed by rapid and dramatic spiritual claims, and he counselled patience with both himself and others in the long, uneven process of sanctification.

He famously compared himself to a person half-rescued from a mud-pit: not yet out, but at least facing the right direction and moving toward cleaner ground. He found the scriptural basis for this patience in Paul’s own testimony: “Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already arrived at my goal, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me” (Philippians 3:12, NIV). This was not an excuse for complacency but a safeguard against the despair that came from expecting instantaneous transformation. The shepherd who understood this could hold his flock through the long middle years of the Christian life with steady, patient hope.

Newton also brought to his pastoral ministry an unusual capacity for bearing with those he disagreed with. He was a Calvinist who refused to use his Calvinism as a weapon; he was an evangelical who maintained pastoral relationships with those of very different theological convictions. He grounded this irenic disposition in Paul’s instruction to Timothy: “And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful. Opponents must be gently instructed, in the hope that God will grant them repentance leading them to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:24–25, NIV). Newton practiced this gentleness not because he had no convictions but because he had learned from his own history that God worked through patience, not through argument, and that a wounded conscience was more likely to be healed by kindness than by doctrinal correctness.

His pastoral ministry of presence — visiting the sick, the dying, the confused, and the grieving — was sustained across eight decades by the simple conviction that every soul he met had been bought by the same blood that had bought his own. He never lost his astonishment at having been forgiven. That astonishment was the wellspring of his pastoral compassion. He loved Paul’s language about the ministry of comfort: “Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4, NIV). Newton had received the comfort. He spent his life distributing it.

He continued to preach at St. Mary Woolnoth well into old age and near-blindness, famously saying when urged to retire: “What! Shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can speak?”

His ministry was a demonstration that pastoral faithfulness is not constrained by age, background, or personal history — that the grace which redeems the vilest sinner is also the grace that qualifies the most unlikely shepherd. He embodied the truth Paul wrote to the Corinthians: “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace to me was not without effect” (1 Corinthians 15:10, NIV). Grace was not without effect in John Newton. It made him one of the most compassionate and effective pastors of his century.

A Prayer

Amazing God, whose grace is greater than any sin we have committed or any darkness we have inhabited, make us pastors who never lose our astonishment at having been forgiven. Where we are tempted to pastor from the height of our holiness, bring us back to the memory of what we were before Your grace found us. Give us Newton’s gentleness with the struggling, his patience with the slow, and his inexhaustible readiness to comfort with the comfort we have ourselves received. Amen.

fields.title: Robert Murray M’Cheyne — The Holy Young Shepherd of Dundee
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Robert Murray M’Cheyne was born on May 21, 1813, in Edinburgh, Scotland, the youngest of five children in a godly middle-class family. He was converted in his early twenties, educated at Edinburgh University and New College, and ordained in 1836 at the age of twenty-three as the first minister of St. Peter’s Church in Dundee — a new church in a working-class district of approximately four thousand people. He ministered there for just seven years before dying of typhus in 1843 at the age of twenty-nine, having never recovered full health after a period of serious illness in 1838–1839. In those seven years he transformed St. Peter’s, wrote hymns that are still sung today, undertook a mission to the Jews of Palestine, and built a prayer movement that outlasted him. Andrew Bonar’s “Memoir and Remains of Robert Murray M’Cheyne,” published after his death, became one of the most widely read Christian biographies of the nineteenth century and a formative influence on generations of ministers.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

M’Cheyne’s understanding of pastoral ministry was summed up in the most famous sentence he ever wrote, addressed to a young ministerial student: “The greatest need of my people is my personal holiness.” This was not a prescription for a withdrawn, other-worldly pietism; it was a pastoral theology of the most practical kind. If the congregation was fed spiritually by the minister, then the spiritual temperature of the congregation was inevitably shaped by the spiritual temperature of the man. A cold-hearted minister produced a cold-hearted congregation. A man in genuine communion with God carried that communion into the pulpit with him, and the congregation felt it.

M’Cheyne grounded this conviction in Paul’s personal exhortation to Timothy, which he regarded as the most important pastoral counsel in the New Testament: “Don’t let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith and in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to preaching and to teaching. Do not neglect your gift… Watch your life and doctrine closely.

Persevere in them, because if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:12–16, NIV). Life and doctrine together, inseparably: the watching of the life first, and then its overflow into the doctrine. M’Cheyne rose early every morning to spend the first hours of the day with God before he met with his people, convinced that an unhurried morning with the Lord was the single most important pastoral preparation he could make.

His pastoral preaching was distinctive in its Christ-centredness. He believed that every passage of Scripture pointed ultimately to Christ and that every sermon, whatever its text, should bring the congregation to the Saviour. He was not interested in moralizing or practical self-improvement separated from the person of Christ; he wanted his people to know and love and trust the Lord Jesus with a depth of personal intimacy that transformed their lives from the inside out. He took to heart Paul’s declaration of pastoral method: “For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2, NIV). This was not intellectual narrowness but pastoral wisdom: in the crucified Christ was the full width of human need — forgiveness, healing, hope, identity, purpose, and eternal life. Everything his congregation needed was there.

M’Cheyne’s pastoral care extended with particular tenderness to the young of his congregation.

He invested heavily in the children and young people of St. Peter’s, building Sunday schools, catechism classes, and young people’s meetings, convinced that the spiritual formation of the next generation was among the most urgent pastoral priorities. He had been converted young himself and understood that the grace which caught him early could catch others early too. He found his model in Paul’s personal investment in Timothy: “I have been reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also” (2 Timothy 1:5, NIV). Faith transmitted through personal relationship across generations was the pattern — and M’Cheyne worked to be that kind of transmitter to the young of Dundee.

His illness in 1838 — which removed him from his congregation for almost a year and which he described with anguish in his diary — was one of the most formative pastoral experiences of his life. In the weakness of that year he came to understand in his body what he had previously understood only in his theology: that the power of ministry did not originate in human strength, and that a weak minister trusting in a strong God could accomplish more than a vigorous minister trusting in himself.

He found in Paul’s experience the language for his own: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9, NIV).

The greatest revival in St. Peter’s history occurred while M’Cheyne was absent — led by William C. Burns during his convalescence. He received this news with humble joy, understanding it as a confirmation that the work had never been his to begin with.

M’Cheyne died at twenty-nine. He left behind him a transformed congregation, a body of hymns, a pattern of personal devotion that has shaped ministers across the world, and a famous Bible-reading plan that his friend Andrew Bonar published and which is still in use today — carrying readers through the whole Bible in a year, the Old Testament once and the New Testament twice.

He had planted in seven years what many ministries do not plant in fifty. He embodied Peter’s vision of what the pastoral life produces: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light” (1 Peter 2:9, NIV). He had declared those praises. His congregation declared them after him. And the declaration has not stopped.

A Prayer

Holy Lord, remind us that the greatest thing we can do for our congregations is to be holy ourselves. Where we have substituted activity for communion, busyness for devotion, or technique for holiness, restore us. Make us like M’Cheyne — men whose first hours belong to You, whose preaching is saturated with Christ, and whose greatest ambition is not a large ministry but a holy one. And let us trust that if the work is truly Yours, it will outlast us. Amen.

fields.title: A.W. Tozer — The Prophet in the Pulpit
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Aiden Wilson Tozer was born on April 21, 1897, on a farm in Newburg, Pennsylvania, and converted to Christianity at age seventeen after hearing a street preacher in Akron, Ohio. He was entirely self-educated in theology — he never attended seminary or college — and was ordained as a minister in the Christian and Missionary Alliance in 1920. He served as pastor of Chicago’s Southside Alliance Church from 1928 to 1959 — thirty-one years — and then at Avenue Road Church in Toronto until his death in 1963 at sixty-six. He edited “Alliance Life” magazine for many years and authored over forty books, the most celebrated of which is “The Pursuit of God” (1948), widely regarded as a Christian classic. He was known as a “prophetic voice” in the evangelical church of his era — a man willing to say what others would not, who saw the church’s compromises clearly and named them plainly.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Tozer’s pastoral vision was that of the prophet-pastor: the man who does not merely manage a religious institution but guards the spiritual integrity of the community he serves. He was deeply concerned throughout his ministry that American evangelicalism was in danger of exchanging the authentic pursuit of God for a comfortable religious experience that demanded nothing and transformed no one. His books and sermons were acts of pastoral alarm — urgent, sometimes sharp, always rooted in the conviction that the church of Jesus Christ was meant to be something far more serious and far more glorious than what most of its members had settled for.

But he was a man seriously in pursuit of a perfect God — and his pursuit called his congregation to the same.

Consuming God, deliver us from the pastoral safety of saying only what our congregations want to hear. Give us Tozer’s courage to speak what the Spirit is actually saying, even when it is uncomfortable. fields.title: Dietrich Bonhoeffer — The Pastor Who Counted the Cost
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born on February 4, 1906, in Breslau, Germany, into a cultured, upper-middle-class family of physicians, lawyers, and academics. He showed exceptional intellectual gifts from childhood and completed his theological doctorate at the University of Berlin at the age of twenty-one. After a formative year in New York at Union Theological Seminary and Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem — where he encountered an African-American Christianity of spiritual depth that he believed German Lutheranism had largely lost — he returned to Germany to teach, preach, and eventually lead the illegal “Confessing Church” seminary at Finkenwalde in defiance of the Nazi-controlled German church. He was arrested by the Gestapo in April 1943, imprisoned for two years at Tegel Prison in Berlin, and executed by hanging at Flossenbürg concentration camp on April 9, 1945 — three weeks before the end of the war. His books, including “The Cost of Discipleship” and “Life Together,” have shaped Christian thought across the world for eight decades.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Bonhoeffer’s pastoral vision was born in a crisis. The German church of the 1930s was, with notable exceptions, capitulating to National Socialism — allowing the state to dictate its doctrine, purge its Jewish-Christian members, and press its ministry into the service of national ideology. Bonhoeffer’s response was to insist, at increasing personal cost, that the church of Jesus Christ owed its ultimate obedience not to the state but to its Lord, and that pastoral ministry meant, in conditions of crisis, the willingness to suffer for that confession rather than compromise it.

His foundational text for pastoral ministry was the account of Christ’s call in the synoptic Gospels, which he unpacked at length in The Cost of Discipleship. The call of Jesus was absolute and unconditional: it demanded a break with every prior loyalty, every prior security, every prior identity. Bonhoeffer identified what he called “cheap grace” — the preaching of forgiveness without repentance, baptism without church discipline, and the Lord’s Supper without confession — as the most dangerous corruption facing the German church.

Against it he set the words of Jesus: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will find it” (Matthew 16:24–25, NIV). The pastor who preached cheap grace was not offering his congregation a gentle version of Christianity; he was offering them a counterfeit that would fail them at the very moment they most needed the real thing.

His Life Together — a short, luminous account of the community life at his Finkenwalde seminary — was his pastoral theology of Christian community. He argued that the Christian community must be built not on human affinity, shared temperament, or institutional convenience but on the Word of God and on the person of Jesus Christ alone. Any community built on human foundations would eventually collapse when human failings became too great to bear. Only a community grounded in Christ could sustain genuine forgiveness, genuine honesty, and genuine love. He found the pattern in Paul’s description of the body: “Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12, NIV). The pastor’s task was to build that body — not to create a collection of satisfied individual consumers.

Bonhoeffer’s pastoral courage in the face of state pressure was one of the most searching exhibitions of pastoral integrity in the twentieth century. He had the opportunity to remain in the safety of America when the war began; instead he returned to Germany, knowing what it might cost him. He believed that the pastor’s authority rested ultimately on his willingness to suffer for the truth he proclaimed — that a shepherd who ran when the wolves came was not a shepherd at all. He held to Hebrews’ charge to congregations: “Have confidence in your leaders and submit to their authority, because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account. Do this so that their work will be a joy, not a burden, for that would be of no benefit to you” (Hebrews 13:17, NIV). He gave his congregation reason for confidence by being the kind of shepherd described here — one who kept watch at the cost of his own freedom and, ultimately, his life.

His prison writings, collected in Letters and Papers from Prison, display a pastoral sensibility that continued to function even in conditions designed to destroy it. He wrote letters of genuine spiritual direction to family and friends from his cell. He led worship services for fellow prisoners and guards. He found in Paul’s prison letters — Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians — not merely consolation but a model of pastoral ministry conducted from within the most constraining circumstances imaginable. He had absorbed what Paul testified: “I can do all this through him who gives me strength” (Philippians 4:13, NIV). The all things he could do through Christ included dying well, which he did — according to the camp physician who witnessed his execution — with composure and serenity that astonished even the guards.

His legacy is the legacy of the pastor who refused to separate theological conviction from ethical action, who understood that the church’s silence in the face of injustice was itself a pastoral failure, and who paid for this understanding with his life. He had preached Amos and Micah with great power; he died exemplifying what he had preached. He had taken Peter’s vision of the pastoral calling with complete seriousness: “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them — not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be” (1 Peter 5:2, NIV). He was willing. He was willing to the end.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, who laid down Your life for Your sheep, make us shepherds willing to do the same. Where the church is tempted to offer cheap grace, give us Bonhoeffer’s courage to preach the cost of discipleship. Where the world’s pressure pushes us toward comfortable silence, give us voices that cannot be quieted. And where the pastoral calling leads us through its own valley of shadows, sustain us with the certainty that You have walked it before us. Amen.

fields.title: Martyn Lloyd-Jones — The Doctor Who Healed Souls
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

David Martyn Lloyd-Jones was born on December 20, 1899, in Cardiff, Wales, the son of a dairy farmer who later moved the family to London. He showed extraordinary academic gifts and trained as a physician, becoming in his mid-twenties the junior assistant to Sir Thomas Horder, physician to the royal family and the most distinguished clinician in England. He appeared destined for the heights of British medicine. Instead, in 1927, he resigned his medical career, took a dramatic cut in income, and became pastor of a small, struggling Congregational church in Aberavon, South Wales — a working-class mining community. He served there for eleven years before accepting the call to Westminster Chapel in London in 1938, where he preached for the next thirty years to congregations of several thousand people. His Friday-night Bible studies and his long expository sermon series — including thirteen years on Paul’s letter to the Romans — produced a body of published sermons that remains among the most widely read in the English-speaking world. He died in 1981 at eighty-one.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Lloyd-Jones’ pastoral vision was shaped by his medical training in ways that he acknowledged throughout his ministry. The physician’s method — careful diagnosis before prescription, attention to underlying causes rather than surface symptoms, refusal to offer a remedy that addressed only the presenting complaint while leaving the deeper disease untouched — was, he believed, precisely the method required of the faithful pastor-preacher. The congregation that was given comfort without diagnosis was like a patient sent away with pain medication when what they needed was surgery. The pastor-physician’s first obligation was to the truth of the condition, not to the comfort of the patient.

Lloyd-Jones’ deepest conviction about preaching — which he regarded as the primary pastoral act — was that it was not merely the communication of information or even of doctrine but an event in which God Himself spoke through His Word to the gathered congregation. He had a theology of the preached Word as the living voice of God, grounded in Paul’s description of the gospel’s reception in Thessalonica: “And we also thank God continually because, when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as it actually is, the word of God, which is indeed at work in you who believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:13, NIV). The Word was at work — not the preacher, not the sermon, but the Word itself, living and active in those who received it. The preacher’s task was to get out of the way of that working and let the Word do what only the Word could do.

His great sermon series, particularly his exposition of Romans, was a sustained act of pastoral care for the whole person. He believed that doctrinal preaching, properly done, was not the opposite of pastoral warmth but its deepest expression — because the people who understood the doctrines of grace, justification, and sanctification most clearly were the people best equipped to endure suffering, resist temptation, and sustain faith under pressure. He grounded this in Paul’s own statement of method: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile. For in the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed” (Romans 1:16–17, NIV). The gospel in its full doctrinal richness was not a liability to be managed but a power to be released. His thirty years of expository preaching were thirty years of releasing that power.

Lloyd-Jones was deeply concerned, like Tozer, with what he saw as the trivialization of Christian worship in the mid-twentieth century. He believed that the church had progressively substituted human activity for divine encounter — that prayer meetings had become planning meetings, worship services had become performances, and evangelism had become salesmanship. He called the church back to Acts’ description of the earliest community: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles” (Acts 2:42–43, NIV).

Awe was the missing ingredient. A church that had lost its awe before God had lost something essential, and no amount of programming or activity would replace it.

He was equally insistent that the pastor must preach the whole counsel of God, including its most demanding and uncomfortable dimensions. He found Paul’s Miletus address to the Ephesian elders the most searching passage in the New Testament for any man in pastoral office: “For I have not hesitated to proclaim to you the whole will of God. Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood” (Acts 20:27–28, NIV).

The whole will of God: not a curated selection, not the pleasant portions, not the parts that would generate a positive response, but everything — preached with the full authority of a man who understood that the price paid for these souls was the blood of the Son of God.

Lloyd-Jones’ pastoral life at Westminster Chapel was one of sustained, unhurried, deep engagement with his congregation through preaching, personal counseling, and prayer. He was often described by those who knew him as a man whose presence carried a quality of spiritual weight — not severity, but gravity, the gravity of a man who lived before God and knew it. He had absorbed what the author of Hebrews commanded: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles. And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us, fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2, NIV). He ran with perseverance. He fixed his eyes on Jesus. He finished the race. And the congregation he left behind was richer for every year he had served them.

A Prayer

Lord of the Word and the Spirit, make us pastors who are not ashamed of the full gospel and who refuse to offer our congregations comfortable substitutes for the real thing. Give us Lloyd-Jones’ patience for the long work of expository preaching, his diagnostic eye to see what our people truly need, and his holy gravity — the weight of a man who knows he stands between the living Word and its dying hearers. May our ministries be measured not by size but by faithfulness to the whole will of God. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion: The Chief Shepherd Still Calls
fields.body_html:
You have now spent time with ten men who understood the pastoral calling with a seriousness that rebukes every comfortable version of ministry that has arisen since their day. Chrysostom sold the bishop’s palace and went to his death rather than flatter the powerful. Gregory governed the Western church with the title “Servant of servants.” George Herbert transformed his small parish in three years and died before he could see the harvest. Richard Baxter visited every family in Kidderminster and watched a town become a congregation. Jonathan Edwards preached the whole counsel of God to his people for twenty-three years and was dismissed for doing so with integrity. John Newton spent a lifetime distributing the grace that had, against all reason, found him. Robert Murray M’Cheyne poured out a holy ministry in seven years and died at twenty-nine. A.W. Tozer spent thirty-one years in one Chicago church refusing to preach what the age wanted to hear. Dietrich Bonhoeffer returned from safety into danger, built a community of genuine discipleship, and died with serenity on the gallows. Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached the whole letter to the Romans over thirteen years and trusted the Word to do what only the Word could do.

What do these ten men call us to? They call us, first and above all, to seriousness about the pastoral office. The care of souls is not a profession to be managed or a career to be advanced. It is a calling to be discharged, at whatever personal cost, with faithfulness to the One who issued it. The flock does not belong to the pastor; it was bought with blood that is not his, entrusted to him by a Shepherd whose standards are those of a Father who gave His Son for each individual sheep. To handle that responsibility carelessly is an act of theological negligence that these ten men would not recognize as pastoral ministry at all.

They also call us to the comfort of a promise. The Chief Shepherd is still present. The same God who equipped Chrysostom to face exile, who gave Gregory wisdom to care for eight hundred different kinds of people, who sustained M’Cheyne in illness, who walked with Bonhoeffer into the darkness of Flossenbürg — that God is the God who calls every pastor today and promises to equip every person He calls. The author of Hebrews expresses it with breathtaking completeness: “Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with everything good for doing his will, and may he work in us what is pleasing to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever” (Hebrews 13:20–21, NIV). The great Shepherd of the sheep is present.

He is equipping. He is working. The pastoral calling is not a solo venture between a man and his congregation; it is a collaboration between a human under-shepherd and the divine Chief Shepherd, who never sleeps, never abandons His flock, and never runs out of the grace His servants need.

Perhaps you are reading this book as a pastor who is exhausted. The work is long, the fruit is sometimes invisible, and the weight of the souls in your care presses on you in ways that others around you cannot fully understand. The ten men in this book knew that weight. They did not carry it by being extraordinary; they carried it by returning repeatedly to the One who had called them to carry it, distributing it into hands strong enough to bear it. They prayed, they studied, they stayed, and they trusted.

Perhaps you are reading this as someone who is not yet in pastoral office but who feels the first stirrings of a call. The same Shepherd who called these ten is still calling. He is still looking for men and women who will receive His flock with reverence, tend it with patience, guard it with courage, and return it to Him at the last with the words “Here are the ones You gave me, and I have not lost one of them.” That is the pastoral ambition worth having.

The call has not changed. The flock still needs feeding, protecting, and leading. The wolves are still real. The wandering sheep are still wandering. And the Chief Shepherd is still speaking the same commission He has spoken in every generation: “Take care of my sheep” (John 21:16, NIV). Three words. Enough for a lifetime. The ten men in this book gave their lifetimes to it.

May we do the same.

“I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will lead you with knowledge and understanding.”

— Jeremiah 3:15 (NIV)
